title: Slow API Investigation Workflow
description: Follow a repeatable workflow to diagnose slow API endpoints, from measuring the baseline to profiling the hot path and verifying the fix.

data.text: When users report a slow endpoint, the natural instinct is to jump into the code. Experienced engineers start with data: they establish a baseline, isolate the layer, profile the hot path, and change one thing at a time. A systematic workflow turns a frustrating mystery into a repeatable process.

Before changing anything, gather numbers. Use `curl`, `k6`, or a load testing tool to measure p50, p95, and p99 latency. Capture the result in a tool like BenchmarkDotNet or a spreadsheet so you can compare later. Know whether the slowness is constant, gradual, or traffic-dependent.

data.title: Quick Baseline with curl
data.content: Run multiple requests and calculate average and worst-case latency.
data.code:
curl -o /dev/null -s -w "%{time_total}\n" https://api.example.com/orders

# For more robust data, use wrk or k6:
wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s https://api.example.com/orders

data.text: Add coarse-grained timing around middleware, the controller action, and outbound calls. If the action itself is fast but the total request is slow, look at database queries, serialization, or network I/O. If the action is slow, profile the C# code inside it.

data.title: Questions to Ask
items: Is the endpoint slow for all users or only some parameter values?
Does latency grow with payload size or database result set size?
Are downstream services also slow, or is the problem isolated?
Did a recent deployment correlate with the regression?

data.text: Use `dotnet-trace` or Visual Studio Profiler to find CPU hot paths. Use EF Core logging to see which queries run and how long they take. If you have distributed tracing enabled, follow the trace to the slowest span. Do not optimize without evidence—you may fix the wrong thing.

Change one variable at a time: an index, a query, a caching policy, or an async boundary. After each change, re-run your baseline measurement. If latency drops, you have confirmation. If it does not, revert and try a different hypothesis. Document the root cause so the next engineer does not repeat the investigation.

data.title: Change One Thing at a Time
data.text: Changing multiple variables at once makes it impossible to know which fix worked. Small, isolated changes with before-and-after measurements are the hallmark of a good investigation.

data.title: Before and After: N+1 Query
data.content: Replace an N+1 query pattern with a single projection query.

data.title: Key Takeaway
points: Establish a baseline with real traffic or realistic load before changing anything.
Isolate the layer: middleware, action, query, serialization, or external call.
Profile with the right tool: dotnet-trace for CPU, EF Core logs for queries, traces for distributed flows.
Change one thing, measure, and document the result.
data.takeaway: A repeatable workflow beats guessing. Measure, isolate, profile, fix, verify.
